title: Cathy Engelbert Retires as WNBA Commissioner; Successor Search Begins
dek: WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert announced Friday, September 4, 2026, that she will step down at year-end after seven years leading the league. Her tenure saw two major labor negotiations, three new team entries, and higher salaries, but was marked by player criticism over leadership and handling of abuse allegations.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Engelbert, the league's first commissioner since 2019, will retire at the conclusion of 2026, with succession planning already underway through a list of internal and external candidates.
bottom_line: The league must name a successor by December 31, 2026, or Engelbert extends her tenure into 2027. The decision of whether that successor comes from within the league office (likely Head of League Operations Sherrie Deans, per reported candidacy) or from outside, and whether the next commissioner is a former player, as the WNBA has never had one, will signal the league's priorities as it enters expansion and aims to repair the credibility gaps player leadership flagged.
body:
WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert announced her retirement effective at the end of 2026, concluding a seven-year tenure marked by labor gains for players, expansion, and sustained financial growth alongside persistent criticism from athletes and staff. NBA Commissioner Adam Silver, who hired Engelbert in 2019 as the league's first commissioner, announced the decision on Friday, September 4.
Engelbert presided over two major collective bargaining negotiations. The most recent agreement, finalized earlier in 2026, raised the salary cap to $7 million, created the first million-dollar salaries in league history, and established the first comprehensive revenue-sharing model in women's professional sports. Under her leadership, three new teams entered the league, the Golden State Valkyries, Portland Fire, and Toronto Tempo, with three more set to join by 2030 in Cleveland, Detroit, and Philadelphia, bringing the total to 18 teams. Sponsorships, media-rights valuations, and team valuations expanded significantly during her tenure.
In a letter to players, Engelbert said: "I retire knowing we have built something bigger, stronger and more enduring than we could have imagined." She told the Associated Press: "It's a good time to hand it off to the next leader to take the 'W' into a better phase. I'm proud of the team we built and everything we accomplished. A leader knows when it's time to drop the mic and move on after building a powerhouse team in the league office." Engelbert indicated she would remain in office into 2027 if a successor is not named by year-end.
Her tenure was shadowed by player dissent over leadership and handling of sensitive matters. Minnesota Lynx forward Napheesa Collier said before the 2026 CBA talks, per Front Office Sports reporting: "We have the best players in the world. We have the best fans in the world, but right now we have the worst leadership in the world." Critics cited Engelbert's handling of racial abuse toward players, the $75 million capital raise in 2022 that sold off 16 percent of the league, and the decision to relocate the Connecticut Sun to Houston. When asked at the WNBA draft this spring about her status, Engelbert responded: "I wonder whether you would ask that of a man, by the way, but I realize as women we get asked different questions than men do."
WNBPA Executive Director Terri Carmichael Jackson said in a statement: "We didn't always agree, but we absolutely shared a belief in what this league could become and in building a better future for the women at the heart of it. I'm proud of what we were able to accomplish together and, on behalf of our player membership, I wish Cathy and her family nothing but the best in whatever she chooses to do next." WNBPA President Nneka Ogwumike, herself retiring after this season, said: "Leading through this much change is no small undertaking, and I have great respect for the commitment Cathy brought to the role."
Silver said in a statement: "Cathy has presided over the WNBA through the most significant period of growth in the league's 30-year history. We are grateful for Cathy's leadership and unwavering commitment to the advancement of women's basketball."  She will lead the search for her successor from among internal and external candidates already submitted to league owners, though Silver has final say on the appointment.
